# Haplotype-based methods









## Theme of this chapter

All of our exercises so far focused on population genetic statistics which are
generally thought about in terms of allele frequencies and allele frequency
correlations. However, one class of modeling tools implemented in _slendr_ which
are also extremely useful are methods based on haplotypes---i.e., continuous
segments of DNA inherited from generation to generation while being broken up by
the process of recombination.

To make this session a little more relaxed compared to previous exercises, this
chapter presents these techniques as a set of "recipes" rather than extensive
exercises. The primary goal is to conclude our exercise sessions with a few more
tools before we switch gears and start implementing modeling workflows for your
own projects or work through some of the few suggested case studies.










## Preparation

**Take a look at the following basic admixture model, and save it as
`haplotypes.R`. Note also the presence of a small helper function I provided
(you don't have to study it, although it should look familiar if you've done the
_tidyverse_ and _ggplot2_ parts of this workbook):**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the entire script

```{r}
#| message: false
#| collapse: true
##################################################
# simple admixture demographic model
library(slendr)
init_env()

popZ <- population("popZ", time = 3000, N = 500)
popX <- population("popX", time = 1500, N = 2000, parent = popZ)
popY <- population("popY", time = 1500, N = 10000, parent = popZ)

gf <- gene_flow(from = popX, to = popY, proportion = 0.2, start = 500, end = 499)

model <- compile_model(list(popZ, popX, popY), generation_time = 1, gene_flow = gf)

schedule <- rbind(
  schedule_recording(model, times = seq(1400, 0, by = -200), list(popY, 10)),
  schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(popX, 10), list(popZ, 10))
)
  
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = 42) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 42)

samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

##################################################
# a helper function to plot admixture tracts

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(scales)

plot_tracts <- function(tracts, ind) {
  ind_tracts <- filter(tracts, name %in% ind) %>%
    mutate(chr = paste0(name, "\nchr. ", haplotype)) %>%
    mutate(chr = factor(chr, levels = unique(chr[order(node_id)])))

  ggplot(ind_tracts) +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = left, xmax = right, ymin = 1, ymax = 2, fill = name),
              linewidth = 1) +
    labs(x = "coordinate along a chromosome [bp]") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
    facet_grid(chr ~ .) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma)
}
```

:::

Here is what this model look like. Note particularly the "ancient DNA time
series" we simulated in `popY` and the admixture from `popX` into `popY`:

```{r}
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule, proportions = TRUE)
```











## Exercise: Local ancestry inference (LAI) with `ts_tracts()`

As mentioned above, we've learned a lot about admixture tests based on allele
frequency correlations, namely $f$-statistics. Although very powerful, there are
situations where they either lose inference power or they don't allow us to
answer deeper questions we might be also interested in.

For instance, **what if we want to detect not only _if_ or _how much_ admixture
happened, but _where_ in the genome can we detect continuous admixture blocks?**

**A wide range of software methods called Local Ancestry Inference (LAI) have
been developed do do exactly this**, each with their strengths and weaknesses.
For an overview, see [this
preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.05.19.725905v1) which I
put together with a former PhD student about LAI methods (fun fact: _slendr_ is
what made this work possible!).

**On the simulation side, _slendr_ provides a function `ts_tracts()`, which can
extract the exact coordinates of admixture tracts resulting an admixture
event.** This is extremely useful both for simulation-based inference, but also
for benchmarking software methods, picking which method gives the most accurate
answer in our scenario of interest, etc.

---

**If you have a simulated tree sequence `ts`** (such as the one simulated by
your script `haplotypes.R`)**, you can obtain admixture tracts by providing a
so-called "census time" to the function `ts_tracts()`** (this is a slightly
strange name for a [low-level technical
concept](https://tskit.dev/msprime/docs/stable/ancestry.html#census-events)
corresponding to the time of gene-flow we want to focus on). **In case of our
model, set this `census` to 500 generations and add the following command to
your script `haplotypes.R`, then run it. What's the format of the data it gives
you? Can you guess what sort of information it contains by looking through it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| output: false
tracts <- ts_tracts(ts, census = 500)
```

When you look at the output of this function, you seen that it's a plain data
frame with many columns which will be familiar to you:

```{r}
head(tracts)
```

For instance, `name` indicates the name of the individual carrying a given
admixture tract derived from admixture from source population `source_pop` with
genomic coordinates between `left` and `right`.

:::

---

**Can you guess the meaning of the `haplotype` column? How many of them are
there for any given individual? You can use your _tidyverse_ magic to answer
this.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

This finds the haplotype number and node ID for each individual:

```{r}
tracts %>% group_by(name) %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)
```

Haplotype is basically equivalent to "chromosome" in this case. Because each
simulated _slendr_ individual is diploid, we get one "chromosome" for each of
them. The `node_id` column is a low-level numerical identifier for such
chromosome used by the underlying _tskit_ Python module which handles
tree-sequence operations.

Here are both columns for the couple of individuals separately, making it clear
that there are always two entries for each of them:

```{r}
tracts %>% group_by(name)  %>% filter(name == "popY_71") %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)
tracts %>% group_by(name)  %>% filter(name == "popY_80") %>% distinct(haplotype, node_id)
```

:::

---

In the script above, I provided the function `plot_tracts()` for you. The way it
works is that you give it a table of all `tracts` and the names of some
individuals recorded in the tree sequence.

You can probably guess what this function does. **To test this function, give it
the simulated `tracts` data frame and a vector of names of individuals who span
a wider range of "aDNA time points", starting from the oldest individual and
ending by an individual "from the present day" (but no more than one individual
from each time point, just to keep things manageable).**

**What do you see in terms of the number of tracts and the length of tracts
across these individuals? Can you detect some distinctive pattern or differences
between the individual tracts (even just visually, we'll do this more rigorously
later)?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's apply some _tidyverse_ table munging to select individuals of different
times(remember, we recorded oldest individuals at 1000 generations ago, the
youngest individuals at 0 generations ago). Of course, you could also do this
manually, but this is more effective, particularly if we needed to subsample
many individuals.

```{r}
names <- tracts %>% group_by(time) %>% distinct(name) %>% slice_sample(n = 1) %>% pull(name)
names
```

We then simply provide these names to the helper function:

```{r}
#| width: 800
#| height: 1000
plot_tracts(tracts, names)
```

It looks like the older individual is, the closer they lived to the start of the
admixture event, and the longer the tracts they carry will be. Which makes
perfect sense!

:::

---

If we were interested in benchmarking some inference methods (all of which produce
data very similar to the `tracts` table), this is the ground truth we would be
comparing its performance against---effectively the results of "the perfect method"
which never makes a mistake.

We'll give a tip on how to do this benchmarking in practice in the final
exercise of this chapter.


## Exercise: Dating admixture events

Once we have a set of admixture tracts (either simulated or inferred
empirically), we can try to date the admixture event. Again, we simulated our
tracts and so we know this admixture date exactly, of course. But that's not the
point here. Typically what we want to do is to simulate genomic data (see the
final exercise) from our model, and then use this data as an input to external
inference software to ask the question: How well can this software infer the
truth? An example of such software is
[DATES](https://elifesciences.org/articles/77625),
[MOSAIC](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/212/3/869/5931232), or
[FLARE](https://cell.com/ajhg/retrieve/pii/S0002929722005444).

Still, let's do a little theoretical exercise to demonstrate how admixture tract
coordinates can be used to infer admixture times. In fact, this is not far from
how the methods mentioned above actually do this, so it's quite useful to know
even besides intellectual curiosity.

---

**First, compute the average length of a ancestry tracts in individuals recorded
in each time point, then visualize the length distribution of these tracts stratified
by their length (i.e., assign a color to each distribution).**

**Hint:** You only need a little bit of _tidyverse_ and _ggplot2_ knowledge to
do this. Take a look at the relevant chapters on the left if you need a
refresher. We did something similar with our example IBD data set.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's compute the average length in each time bin:

```{r}
tracts %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(mean(length))
```

Obviously, we can see that the older the individual, the closer to the admixture
event that individual is and, consequently, the longer the admixture tracts are.
This is, of course, because recombination hadn't yet had the time to break up
longer admixture chunks into shorter pieces.

We can get a better idea about this by plotting the admixture tract length
distributions like this:

```{r}
ggplot(tracts, aes(length, color = factor(time))) +
  geom_density() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3e6)) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_discrete("Time of\nrecording") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of admixture lengths, stratified by age group",
       x = "admixture tract length [bp]")
```

:::

---

**Suppose we only have sequences of present-day individuals. In our script,
let's subset the `tracts` data frame to only individuals recorded at time 0 ("the present day"):**

```{r}
tracts <- filter(tracts, time == 0)
```

---

When we look again at the distribution of tracts lengths observed in individuals
at time 0 a bit more carefully, we can notice that it seems to follow the
[exponential
distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution):

```{r, echo=FALSE}
h_ind <- tracts %>% .$length %>% hist(breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)
plot(as.integer(h_ind$mids), h_ind$counts, main = "Tract lengths in individuals at time 0",
     xlab = "tract length bin [bp]", ylab = "count",
     xlim = c(0, max(h_ind$mids)), ylim = c(0, max(h_ind$counts)))
```

[Exponential
distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution) is
governed by the following density function with a _rate parameter_ $\lambda$:

$$
f(\textrm{tract length }~x) \sim \lambda \exp^{-\lambda x}
$$

In the case of exponential decay of admixture tracts and after making some
simplifying assumptions, the $\lambda$ rate parameter can be parametrized as:

$$ \lambda = \frac{1}{r t}, $$ where $r$ is the recombination rate and $t$ is
the time (in generations) since the admixture event.

The [expected
value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution#Mean,_variance,_moments,_and_median)
of such exponential distribution is given by:

$$
\mathop{\mathbb{E}} [X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}
$$

Because we can get the maximum likelihood value of this expected average simply
by computing a simple mean of tract lengths $\bar{x}$, we can also write:

$$
\bar{x} \approx \mathop{\mathbb{E}} [X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}.
$$

Simply by rearranging this equation, we can therefore get an estimate the rate
of exponential decay $\hat{\lambda}$ of the underlying exponential distribution
of the tract lengths as:

$$
\hat{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\bar{x}}.
$$

We can also verify our assumptions by overlaying a theoretical exponential
distribution density corresponding to the tract length data. (This is a very technical bit, so feel free to skip this):

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

We can do this using the `dexp()` function:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# get tract lengths as a normal vector
tract_lengths <- tracts$length

# bin the lengths into 50 bins
h_ind <- hist(tract_lengths, breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)

# plot the length bins (distribution of the data)
plot(as.integer(h_ind$mids), h_ind$counts, main = "Tract lengths in individuals at time 0",
     xlab = "tract length bin [bp]", ylab = "count",
     xlim = c(0, max(h_ind$mids)), ylim = c(0, max(h_ind$counts)))

# compute the exponential density corresponding to the tract lengths distribution
y_values <- dexp(h_ind$mids, rate = 1 / mean(tract_lengths))

# overlay this exponential density on the data
lines(h_ind$mids, sum(h_ind$counts) * unique(diff(h_ind$mids)) * y_values, lty = 2, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
```

:::

But more importantly, because we know that $\lambda = 1 / (r t)$, assuming we
know the uniform average recombination rate $r$ reasonably well, we can estimate
the time of admixture simply by rearranging this equation to extract the
admixture time $t$ as:

$$
t \approx \frac{\hat{\lambda}}{r}
$$

For example, given a vector of tract lengths in our simulated individuals
"from the present day":


```{r}
head(tracts$length, 10) # ... etc
```

we can estimate the rate of exponential decay $\hat{\lambda}$ like this:

```{r}
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(tracts$length)
lambda_hat
```

and then use this value to estimate of time since admixture in the history of
these individual directly:

```{r}
r <- 1e-8 # recombination rate (crossovers per bp per generation)

admixture_time <- lambda_hat / r # admixture time in "generations before this individual lived"

admixture_time
```

---

You can see that we're a little bit of from the true value of 500 generations
(after all, we only simulated a small part of the genome), but still, hopefully
this gives you a hint of how admixture dating methods work, at least in
principle.

Real-world inference uses mathematical machinery which is a little bit more
sophisticated (usually we deal with filtered tracts, or we don't even have full
haplotypes and can only work with linkage information between individual
alleles), but the general ideas remains the same---fitting an exponential curve
to the information signal left in admixed genomes by the process of
recombination.

## Exercise: Identity-by-Descent segments (IBD)

Another function useful for studying demographic history using haplotypes is
`ts_ibd()`. As the name suggests, this function extracts IBD segments for the
given set of individuals recorded in a tree sequence.

Let's first get the names of individuals "at the present":

```{r}
samples <- ts_recorded(ts) %>% filter(time == 0)
samples
```

**In general, there are two modes of operation for the `ts_ibd()` function
(depending on whether we set its argument `within` or `between`) as outlined
bellow.**

(Additionally, because the IBD data from even a tiny simulation can be
absolutely huge, we typically need to pre-filter which IBDs to extract, for
instance by setting the `maximum_time` argument, which only searches for IBDs
that aren't resulting from a most recent common ancestor (MRCA) not older than
the given time. Alternatively, we also have the option to filter for
`minimum_length`, but see the instructions in `?ts_ibd` for some caveats.)

1. **We can look for IBD segments _within_ a given group of individuals by
providing the names of the group of individuals within which to extract IBD
segments.**

```{r}
ibd_within <- ts_ibd(ts, within = samples$name, maximum_time = 100)
```

Looking at the data, we see a familiar data frame structure again, namely with
pairs of names of two individuals `name1` and `name2` for each IBD segment (each
row of the data frame), the time `tmrca` of the most common ancestor from which
the IBD segment was inherited.

When we summarize how many segments of what average length do we find in our
simulated sample set (a simple metric of relatedness), we can see that the
amount of IBDs follows the $N_e$ of the population in our model: the smaller the
$N_e$, the more related (and with more IBD) we observe in our populations:

```{r}
#| message: false
ibd_within %>%
  group_by(pop1, pop2) %>%
  summarize(ibd_count = n(), ibd_length = mean(length))
```

```{r}
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

2. **We can look for IBD segments _between_ two groups by providing two sets of
individuals.**

Let's first convert our present-day only table of samples into the necessary
format (list of vectors, as we discussed many times before).

```{r}
samples <- split(samples$name, samples$pop)
samples
```


**Let's run `ts_ibd()` with the `between` mode. Notice that we see nothing
between any pair of the three populations if we keep the `maximum_time = 100`
filter present. This makes sense because the splits between the populations (and
their $N_e$) don't allow for such "young" IBD segments to persist. This applies
also to the `popY`-`popX` pair whose demographic history involves a substantial
gene flow event of 20%!**

```{r}
ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popZ", "popX")], maximum_time = 100)
ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popZ", "popY")], maximum_time = 100)
ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 100)
```

**We see the same thing between the `popY`-`popX` pair even when we filter for IBD
segments inherited right at the time the gene-flow ended (obviously):**

```{r}
ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 499)
```

**Finally, we do pick up an admixture signal when we allow IBD segments tracing
the MRCA between the two populations to the exact generation during which the
admixture began:**

```{r}
ts_ibd(ts, between = samples[c("popY", "popX")], maximum_time = 500)
```

---

**Unlike every single statistical method introduced in this workshop, there's a
caveat to using `ts_ibd()` used for real-world simulation-based inference of
demographic history or software benchmarking**, and it has to do with [an
issue](https://github.com/tskit-dev/tskit/issues/2459) in how the underlying
_tskit_ tree-sequence machinery handles IBD segments. Read the linked GitHub
issue as well as my note in the `?ts_ibd` help page to learn more.

**That said, if you want to do real-world inference using IBD segments on real
data, this would anyway require applying third-party software doing the
inference anyway (AncIBD, IBDSeq, Ibis, etc.). For this reason, this issue
doesn't have much practical implication.**

**For those applications, let's move on to how you'd go about approaching tying
_slendr_ simulations with external software.**











## Bonus exercise: Converting tree sequences to other genotype formats

As convenient as it is to always work in R with user-friendly modeling interface
of _slendr_, it's library of _tskit_ tree-sequence statistical functions, and
the whole _tidyverse_ and _ggplot2_ data science packages, real-world research
requires using third-party external software. In general, software like this
doesn't work with tree-sequence data structures, and even when it does, our
real-world data doesn't come in the form of tree sequences---it takes the form
of genotype files such as VCF, EIGENSTRAT, PLINK, and others.

Luckily, _slendr_ provides convenient means to convert tree sequences into
standard genotype formats. For instance, if we have a tree sequence object `ts`,
we can:

```{r}
#| echo: false
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

1. **Obtain a VCF file with the function `ts_vcf()`**

```{r}
ts_vcf(ts, path = "/tmp/genotypes.vcf.gz")
```

```{bash}
bcftools view -s popX_1,popY_1,popZ_1 /tmp/genotypes.vcf.gz | head -n15
```

2. **Convert our data into the EIGENSTRAT trio of files for ADMIXTOOLS with the
function `ts_eigenstrat()`**

```{r}
ts_eigenstrat(ts, prefix = "/tmp/eigenstrat")
```

3. **Get a normal table of genotypes as a data frame with the function
`ts_genotypes()`**

```{r}
ts_genotypes(ts)
```

---

With these three functions, you can always finish your _slendr_ simulation
scripts with a file conversion to another fileformat and pick up your inference
work in a different third-party software (IBDseq, DATES, ADMIXTOOLS, PLINK,
etc.).
